statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office – Company Register (online portal at https://www.companiesoffice.govt.nz/companies)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names must use Latin script letters A–Z, Arabic numerals 0–9, and limited punctuation; te reo Māori names are permitted in Latin characters; a non-Latin-script name must be transliterated into Latin script for registration; names must not be offensive or imply a prohibited Crown or government connection under Companies Act 1993, s 20.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A name reservation is valid for 20 working days and may be renewed by filing a fresh reservation application before expiry. If the Registrar declines a requested name, the applicant may file a reconsideration request with the Companies Office within 20 working days, attaching written submissions and any necessary ministerial or regulatory consent. If the reconsideration is unsuccessful, the decision may be appealed by way of judicial review in the High Court of New Zealand under the Judicature Amendment Act 1972.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible for this low-risk non-licensed software business provided the virtual office supplies a physical New Zealand street address (not a PO Box) for service of process, maintains the company's registered office records, and is staffed during ordinary business hours; a mail-forwarding-only virtual office without New Zealand service-of-process capacity is not acceptable.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low risk: approximately 5% annual probability of an unannounced on-site inspection for a clean-screened, low-risk no-code website builder using a compliant registered office. The probability increases to 15–20% annually if a virtual office or nominee-director arrangement is used, due to AML/CFT supervisory inspection powers exercised by the Department of Internal Affairs and the Financial Markets Authority.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: International Companies Act 1981-82 (Cook Islands), as amended by the International Companies Amendment Acts 1991, 2003, 2005 and 2011; incorporating provisions at ss. 5-8 (incorporation and certificate), ss. 11-13 (constitution, memorandum and articles), s. 15 (registered office and registered agent), ss. 18-23 (directors and officers), and ss. 31-36 (share capital and shares); administered in conjunction with the Financial Supervisory Commission Act 2008.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) of the Cook Islands, acting through the Registrar of International Companies, Avarua, Rarotonga, in coordination with licensed international company registered agents.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form IC-1 (Application for Registration of an International Company), filed together with the executed Memorandum and Articles of Association, Form IC-2 (Notice of Registered Office and Registered Agent), director and officer consents, and the statutory declaration of compliance, all submitted electronically by the licensed registered agent.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital is prescribed under the International Companies Act 1981-82. The Memorandum of Association must state the authorised share capital (standard US$10,000 divided into 10,000 ordinary shares of US$1.00 each, or US$50,000 if desired). No escrow, bank deposit, capital contribution, or proof-of-funds condition precedents apply to incorporation; shares may be issued for such consideration as the board determines, including consideration credited as fully paid.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en:
(FORM PRO FORMA) WRITTEN RESOLUTION OF THE FIRST BOARD OF DIRECTORS
OF [●] INTERNATIONAL COMPANY LIMITED
(An International Company incorporated under the International Companies Act 1981-82 of the Cook Islands)

RESOLVED, pursuant to the Memorandum and Articles of Association and the International Companies Act 1981-82 (as amended), that:

1. SHARE SUBSCRIPTION AND ALLOTMENT. The subscription by the initial shareholder for 10,000 ordinary shares of US$1.00 each is accepted; such shares are allotted and issued as fully paid, and the aggregate subscription amount of US$10,000 is credited to the issued share capital account of the Company.

2. ADOPTION OF REGISTERED OFFICE AND REGISTERED AGENT. The registered office of the Company shall be at [●], Rarotonga, Cook Islands, being the office of the licensed registered agent [●]; and [●] is hereby appointed as the registered agent of the Company, with full authority to accept service of process and to maintain the statutory records in accordance with the Act.

3. APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR AND OFFICERS. [●] is appointed as the sole director of the Company; [●] is appointed as President; [●] is appointed as Secretary-Treasurer; each appointment is effective immediately and continues until resignation, death or removal pursuant to the Articles.

4. ADOPTION OF CONSTITUTION AND SEAL. The Memorandum and Articles of Association filed at incorporation are ratified and adopted as the constitution of the Company; the corporate seal (if adopted) shall be held by the Secretary and affixed only under board authority.

5. BANK ACCOUNTS AND COMMERCIAL AGREEMENTS. The officers are authorised to open and operate bank, merchant, and payment-processor accounts, and to execute agreements with Stripe Billing, Paddle, hosting providers and customers for the operation of the visual web template and low-code web application builder business, together with all ancillary contracts and user terms.

6. STATUTORY RECORDS AND FILINGS. The share register, register of directors, minute book, and beneficial ownership register shall be established and maintained at the registered office; the directors are authorised to make all filings, annual returns, and beneficial ownership declarations required by the Financial Supervisory Commission and the Act.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Engagement of Licensed Registered Agent and Client Due Diligence
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Licensed international company registered agent accredited by the Financial Supervisory Commission of the Cook Islands
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Engage a registered agent licensed under Section 15 of the International Companies Act 1981-82 and the Financial Supervisory Commission Act 2008. Complete the agent's client-acceptance file, comprising corporate due diligence (CDD), know-your-client (KYC), and source-of-wealth documentation for each director, shareholder, and ultimate beneficial owner, including any underlying international trust. Provide the proposed company name, intended authorised share capital, and director preferences. The agent issues an engagement letter, collects the government fees, and initiates the incorporation workflow.
required_dossiers: Certificate of incorporation of any parent entity (if the shareholder is a corporate vehicle)
Copy of trust deed and certificate of trustee appointment (if the shareholder is a trust)
Passport or national identity document of each director, shareholder, and ultimate beneficial owner
Proof of residential address (utility bill or bank statement dated within the last 3 months)
Bank reference letter and professional reference
Source of funds and source of wealth declaration
Completed KYC questionnaire and CDD forms of the licensed registered agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the agent or the Financial Supervisory Commission queries the CDD pack, supplement the file with notarised explanations, strengthened source-of-wealth evidence, or a corporate structure chart; any refusal or query must be cured within 14 days of notification to continue the application without delay.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of International Companies, Financial Supervisory Commission (acting through the licensed registered agent)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a name reservation request stating the proposed corporate name, which must end with 'International Company', 'Limited', 'Ltd', or an approved abbreviation. The name must not be identical or confusingly similar to a name already registered and must not suggest Government patronage, illegality, or an undesirable purpose. The licensed agent files the reservation with the Registrar and obtains written name clearance.
required_dossiers: Name reservation request form
Licensed agent's consent cover letter
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the proposed name is refused, submit up to three alternative names in a fresh reservation application; the refusal notice does not prejudice a subsequent application, and the first re-submission generally attracts no additional government fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation and Execution of Memorandum and Articles of Association
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Licensed legal counsel and licensed registered agent of the Cook Islands; incorporator
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft the Memorandum and Articles of Association in compliance with Section 12 of the International Companies Act 1981-82. The Memorandum must state the authorised share capital (typically US$10,000 or US$50,000), the corporate name, the registered office clause (care of the licensed agent), and the objects, which for a no-code web application builder are unrestricted digital-commerce objects. Execute the Memorandum and Articles by the incorporator before a witness; each director, officer, and the registered agent executes a consent to act.
required_dossiers: Draft Memorandum and Articles of Association
Consent to act as director (Form IC-D)
Consent to act as secretary or officer (if appointed)
Form IC-2 - Consent and Notice of Registered Agent and Registered Office
Authorised capital and share structure memorandum
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar objects to a constitutional provision, amend the Memorandum and Articles by executing a deed of amendment and re-submit; pre-registration amendments require no shareholder resolution and are processed as a revised filing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing of Form IC-1 and Payment of Government Fees
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of International Companies, Financial Supervisory Commission
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: The licensed agent files the application for registration with the Registrar under Section 8 of the Act. Submit Form IC-1 (Application for Registration of an International Company) together with the executed Memorandum and Articles, Form IC-2, consents of directors and officers, and a statutory declaration confirming compliance with the Act. Pay the government incorporation fee (US$350 for authorised capital up to US$10,000; US$500 for authorised capital above US$10,000) and the first-year annual license fee.
required_dossiers: Form IC-1 (Application for Registration of an International Company)
Executed Memorandum and Articles of Association
Form IC-2 (Notice of Registered Office and Registered Agent)
Director and officer consents
Statutory declaration of the incorporator or licensed agent
Payment of incorporation and first-year annual license fees
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a requisition or query under Section 8(2) of the Act, file a written cure within 21 days addressing the specified defect and, where necessary, re-executed documents; an expedited same-day filing service is available upon payment of the expediting fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of International Companies, Financial Supervisory Commission
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Upon satisfaction of all statutory requirements, the Registrar seals and issues the Certificate of Incorporation stating the corporate name, unique company number, date of incorporation, and the fact that the company is formed with limited liability. The certificate constitutes conclusive evidence of due incorporation under the Act. The licensed agent obtains the original certificate and delivers a certified copy to the client for banking and payment-processor onboarding.
required_dossiers: No further applicant dossiers; the licensed agent collects the original certificate and arranges certified copies and courier delivery
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the certificate contains an error in the corporate name, date, or company number, apply to the Registrar for rectification under Section 9 of the Act, supported by an affidavit of the licensed agent; re-issue is ordinarily completed within 2 business days.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department of New Zealand (IRD) — online portal: Inland Revenue 'myIR' (https://www.ird.govt.nz)
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign entity without a New Zealand fixed establishment that derives New Zealand-source income or is required to register for New Zealand GST must apply to the Inland Revenue for an IRD number using the prescribed application forms (e.g., IR742 for non-resident individuals/companies, or the applicable entity registration form). The application must be lodged with certified constitutional documents, proof of foreign registration, director/beneficial owner identity documentation, and a New Zealand contact address or agent appointment. Upon approval, the IRD issues an 8- or 9-digit IRD number. For GST registration, use the myIR portal or Form IR356; a non-resident may register for GST if it carries on a taxable activity in New Zealand or if it makes remote services supplies to New Zealand consumers unless a reverse-charge or registration-threshold exception applies.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No general check-the-box election exists under New Zealand income tax law. However, an eligible company may elect into the Look-Through Company (LTC) regime (IR61 form and shareholder consents) so that income and losses are treated as transparent for New Zealand tax purposes, subject to the LTC eligibility rules and the requirement that New Zealand-resident shareholders collectively own at least 20% (or, if certain cross-border exceptions apply, the Commissioner may accept the election with appropriate conditions). Additionally, hybrid mismatch rules under Subpart FH of the Income Tax Act 2007 may require a person to make an election to align tax treatment of a foreign hybrid entity or to disapply a mismatch outcome; a New Zealand branch of a foreign company may also elect to use the branch equivalent tax accounts method. A fully foreign-owned International Company with no New Zealand substantive presence will generally be treated as non-resident and not subject to New Zealand income tax on non-New-Zealand-source income; the Tax-Exempt Zone classification reflects the absence of a New Zealand permanent establishment and the statutory exemption of certain offshore income.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) — New Zealand GST Act 1985
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in any 12-month period (or a reasonable expectation of exceeding NZD 60,000 in the next 12 months); non-resident suppliers of remote services to New Zealand consumers have a nexus based on the value of supplies to New Zealand consumers and may be required to register under the GST (Remote Services) rules regardless of the NZD 60,000 threshold unless the supplier is already registered or uses the reverse-charge regime under the MOSS-like simplified registration, subject to the specific rules in section 54C and schedule 3B of the GST Act.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand does not operate a real-time fiscal clearance or mandatory e-invoicing clearance system. Inland Revenue accepts electronic invoices, but there is no API-based stamping or digital fiscal seal obligation for GST. Businesses meeting the turnover threshold must issue tax invoices showing the GST number, supplier and recipient details, description, date, and GST-inclusive/exclusive amounts; buyers may use the buyer-created tax invoice process where permitted. A voluntary electronic invoicing framework based on the Peppol standard exists for public sector procurement, but it is not a statutory GST clearance mandate.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating applies under the GST Act 1985 to exports of goods supplied to a recipient outside New Zealand if the goods are exported from New Zealand within 28 days of the supply, to a supply of goods that is a final export, to certain international transportation and freight services, and to services supplied to a non-resident recipient who is outside New Zealand at the time the services are performed, provided the services are not supplied to a New Zealand resident and are not supplied in connection with land in New Zealand. The 'zero-rating of services' also extends to remote services supplied to non-resident recipients if the services are not performed in New Zealand or the recipient is not in New Zealand at the time of supply. A person must hold sufficient written evidence of the non-resident status of the recipient and the export occurrence; the zero-rating does not apply to services that are physically performed in New Zealand for a non-resident's private use or enjoyment in a manner that gives the non-resident a direct benefit in New Zealand.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: New Zealand Customs Export Declaration (Electronic Customs Export Declaration via the New Zealand Customs Service Trade Single Window)
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill
Evidence of shipment and export within the statutory 28-day window (e.g., cargo movement records, port/terminal receipts)
Inward Remittance Certificate or bank evidence of foreign currency payment for the exported goods
Supplier's GST tax invoice showing the zero-rating basis
A copy of the recipient's non-resident identity evidence (e.g., foreign VAT registration certificate, certificate of incorporation, or passport/address evidence)
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The Commissioner of Inland Revenue may audit export zero-rating claims and require production of all export documentation and remittance evidence. If a taxpayer incorrectly zero-rates a supply or does not retain the required evidence, the supply may be recharacterized as subject to GST at 15%, resulting in a retrospective output tax adjustment, use-of-money interest, and shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994. Shortfall penalties can range from 20% for lack of reasonable care to 150% for evasion or similar acts, plus a criminal penalty of up to NZD 50,000 for a company (and potentially higher fines for individuals) for knowingly providing false or misleading information. Goods exported but not remitted/repatriated within the contractual terms without valid commercial reasons may also signal an artificial arrangement and trigger anti-avoidance provisions, including the general anti-avoidance rule in section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007 and the associated reconstruction powers of the Commissioner.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua) as the apex monetary authority and prudential supervisor in New Zealand; for the associated Cook Islands International Company (CK_IC), the Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) administers licensing, AML/CFT supervision, and financial institution regulation within the Cook Islands, while the Reserve Bank of New Zealand acts as the effective central bank for the Cook Islands because the Cook Islands uses the New Zealand dollar (NZD) and maintains no independent central bank.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand is an IMF Article VIII economy; the NZD is fully convertible in both current-account and capital-account transactions, and there are no exchange controls, no approval requirements, and no quantitative limits on inbound or outbound movements of funds. Capital contributions, shareholder loans, dividends, royalties, and service fees may be remitted freely in any convertible currency, subject only to standard banking AML/CFT due diligence and, where applicable, New Zealand withholding taxes on NZ-source income (notably 15% non-resident withholding tax on dividends and interest absent a treaty or exemption, with no NZ-Cook Islands double tax agreement currently in force). For the no-code website builder operating through Stripe Billing and Paddle, settlement proceeds in USD, EUR, or NZD may be swept into the IC's bank account without prior reserve bank consent; conversion to NZD is available at the interbank market rate less the bank's standard FX spread.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. New Zealand imposes no statutory surrender, conversion, or repatriation timeline for export receipts, SaaS subscription proceeds, or any other form of foreign currency income. Exporters and digital service providers may retain foreign currency balances indefinitely, sell them at prevailing market exchange rates at any time, or denominate invoices in any freely convertible currency. Stripe and Paddle settlement statements should be reconciled monthly to the operating bank account, and any open foreign currency positions should be managed under the entity's documented treasury policy to avoid unintended FX exposure.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: MEDIUM. Offshore digital EMIs such as Wise, Airwallex, Payoneer, and Currencycloud are viable as complementary cross-border payment and disbursement rails, but they cannot replace a Tier-1 New Zealand bank account because Stripe Billing and Paddle settle to a licensed bank account held by the payment aggregator, ultimately remitting to a board-designated operating account rather than to an unlicensed EMI wallet. Legal constraints: any EMI providing money or financial services in New Zealand must be registered on the Financial Service Providers Register under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008 and must implement an AML/CFT programme under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009; offshore EMIs without an NZ FSP registration or without a licensed partner bank may not lawfully solicit or maintain NZ payment services. Recommended treasury design: maintain Wise or Airwallex as automated sweep accounts for recurring supplier payments below NZD 10,000 and for same-day cross-border reconciliation, while the primary liquidity spine remains a Tier-1 NZ bank account; all EMI balances should be capped at NZD 50,000 and drained daily to minimize unsecured counterparty risk.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: In-person or recorded video-conference interview is mandatory. For a non-resident Cook Islands International Company, NZ banks uniformly require: (i) a physical meeting at the branch or a live video identification call for each director and the ultimate beneficial owner before account activation; (ii) certified passport and proof of residential address dated within the last six months; (iii) the Cook Islands corporate extract, certificate of good standing, and register extracts, apostilled; and (iv) if all directors are non-resident, the appointment of a New Zealand-based contact person or licensed corporate services agent for service of documents. Fully remote, digital-only account opening with no human interaction is unavailable for a tax-exempt offshore IC; the onboarding interview typically lasts 45–60 minutes and is repeated for each signatory, with biometric identity capture and independent verification of the beneficial ownership declaration.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cook Islands tax-exempt International Company status flagged under the AML/CFT Act 2009 as an offshore structure with potential shell-company or tax-arbitrage characteristics.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission Certificate of Good Standing; apostilled extract from the Register of International Companies; annual return and board minutes; statutory declaration of active business confirming operation of the no-code website builder; tax residence certificate issued by the Cook Islands Ministry of Finance confirming tax-exempt status; six months of operational receipts from Stripe/Paddle; comprehensive transaction ledger demonstrating real commercial activity.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Opaque or trust-based beneficial ownership structure, creating risk of undisclosed controllers or asset-hiding arrangements.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete register of ultimate beneficial owners with name, date of birth, nationality, and residential address of each natural person holding or controlling 25% or more; trust deed or certified extract identifying settlor, protector, trustee, and beneficiaries; written confirmation from the licensed Cook Islands registered agent confirming identity verification; independent legal opinion confirming the trust has legitimate asset-protection and succession purposes and does not constitute a sham.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Lack of local economic substance in New Zealand (no employees, no physical office, no payroll), typical of letterbox companies.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: New Zealand employment agreements for remote staff or a BPO services contract; virtual office or serviced-office lease in Auckland; platform business evidence including Stripe/Paddle settlement volumes, customer website inventory, and proprietary IP registrations; board resolution designating New Zealand as the APAC treasury centre; GST registration certificate if taxable turnover exceeds NZD 60,000; PAYE filing records; executed customer contracts evidencing the software-as-a-service revenue model.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Inability to evidence the source of initial capital injection, especially where funds originate from a Cook Islands trust bank account.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Six months of bank statements from the originating bank; SWIFT MT103/MT202 transaction records; board resolution authorising the capital injection; subscription agreement or deed-of-settlement documentation; tax audit confirmation or affidavit as to the lawful origin of funds; if the funding derives from a trust distribution, a certified copy of the trustee's distribution resolution and underlying source-of-wealth summary.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant wire protocol: remit via SWIFT MT103 (or MT202 for high-value transfers) from the overseas beneficial owner's or shareholder's bank to the NZ Tier-1 operating account, using the harmonised payment purpose code for equity contribution or capital injection (e.g., the bank-specific New Zealand code for capital account transfers, or narrative text 'Share capital contribution per board resolution dated [date]'). The board resolution, Cook Islands corporate extract, and beneficial ownership declaration must be uploaded to the bank's compliance portal before or immediately after the transfer. No Reserve Bank of New Zealand approval is required; funds are typically credited on the same or next business day after automatic AML screening and destination-country validation. Inbound injections above NZD 100,000 may trigger a source-of-funds questionnaire; third-party remitters are not permitted unless supported by a written loan or assignment agreement, and structured or cash-based transfers must be avoided entirely.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Clearing rails, in priority order: (1) SWIFT MT103 direct transfers for supplier invoices, referencing the commercial invoice number and the applicable purpose code, with FX rate lock executed through the bank's online treasury platform; (2) bank-issued documentary commercial letters of credit (sight and usance) under UCP 600 for procurement of agriculture/food commodities from APAC counterparties, supported by invoice, bill of lading, packing list, and inspection certificate; (3) New Zealand domestic clearings via the RBNZ Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS) and Payments NZ direct credit facilities for salaries, GST payments, and domestic invoices; (4) licensed fintech EMI sweeps via Wise or Airwallex for recurring cross-border disbursements below NZD 10,000, with fallback to SWIFT for any rejected batch; (5) multi-currency netting through the bank's global treasury platform to minimise conversion costs. Each drawdown must be supported by the underlying contract, reconciled against Stripe/Paddle settlement entries, and subjected to enhanced screening where the beneficiary resides in a higher-risk jurisdiction.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable outright forward FX contracts (NZD/USD, NZD/EUR, NZD/AUD) executed under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with a registered NZ bank, used to lock margins on recurring software subscription revenues and to hedge known supplier invoices.
FX swaps (short-tenor spot-to-forward) to manage the staging of capital injections and distribution timing without expanding credit lines.
Cross-currency interest rate swaps (CCS) for notional alignment where the IC holds USD or EUR-denominated receivables through Stripe/Paddle but incurs NZD-denominated operating costs.

Vanilla FX options (purchased calls and puts only; no sold options) for protection against adverse NZD currency movements, permitted for wholesale or eligible investors under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 and subject to completion of the bank's derivatives suitability questionnaire.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) strictly for hedging Asia-Pacific invoice exposure in non-convertible or restricted currencies (e.g., CNY, INR, IDR) where physical delivery is impossible or the underlying counterparty imposes settlement restrictions; where the currency is deliverable, outright forwards are preferred.
Exchange-listed FX futures (CME Group NZD/USD contract) for margin-transparent hedging of a committed three-to-six-month receivables pipeline, collateralised by segregated cash margin.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return and Annual Government Renewal Fee
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of International Companies, Financial Services Development Authority, Cook Islands
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 3 months after each anniversary of the date of incorporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing accrues a late fee and default notice; continued non-compliance after notice causes the company to be struck off the International Companies Register. Directors may be fined under the International Companies Act 2012, and reinstatement, if available, requires payment of all outstanding fees and penalties.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory audit requirement for an International Company not carrying on business in the Cook Islands. No asset/revenue threshold triggers mandatory audit; an independent audit is required only if shareholders elect it or if the company conducts local Cook Islands business.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: No prescribed GAAP for foreign-source activities. If financial statements are voluntarily prepared, IFRS or another internationally recognised GAAP may be used; records must truthfully explain the company's transactions.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: No public UBO register is filed. The registered agent maintains confidential beneficial ownership information for AML/CFT purposes; the annual return confirms the current directors and shareholders, and any share transfer during the year must be recorded contemporaneously in the Register of Members before the next annual confirmation.

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 550 - 1,200 per year for a Cook Islands registered agent and physical registered office
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: Not required by statute; voluntary audit typically USD 5,000 - 12,000 per year

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: New Zealand levies a flat corporate income tax rate of 28% on resident companies. No general statutory tax holidays exist. Preferential deductions and credits include the R&D tax credit (15% of eligible R&D expenditure), the R&D loss tax credit (for loss-making start-ups), the approved innovation partnership deduction, and immediate deductions for certain low-value assets. Under the grey-list CFC and FIF rules, certain foreign-sourced dividends and active business income may be effectively exempt where no New Zealand management and control is exercised. The approved issuer levy (AIL) regime permits a 2% levy in lieu of non-resident withholding tax on certain interest. No specific preferential code-site builder digital tax carve-out applies.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IRD Form IR4 (Company Income Tax Return), filed electronically via Inland Revenue's myIR online portal or through approved software providers.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The IR4 must be filed by the 7th day of the 7th month after the company's balance date. For a 31 March balance date, the deadline is 7 October. Non-standard balance dates require Inland Revenue approval. Provisional taxpayers must also pay terminal tax and provisional tax instalments in line with the standard due dates.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Company legal name and IRD number
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Enter the New Zealand registered name and IRD number. A non-resident company must obtain an NZ IRD number and may file through a New Zealand tax agent.

Include New Zealand-sourced income, and worldwide income if the company is a New Zealand tax resident by incorporation or by having its centre of management and control in New Zealand. Foreign-sourced income derived by a non-resident may be exempt.
Claim only expenses incurred in deriving assessable income. Apply New Zealand transfer pricing adjustments under Subpart GC.
Apply thin capitalisation rules (sections FE 1–FE 18) where a non-resident-owned company's debt percentages exceed allowable thresholds.
Only legally deductible items; non-resident entities rarely claim donations unless made from assessable income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income before loss offsets
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Compute under the Income Tax Act 2007. Loss-making companies may carry losses forward subject to shareholder continuity tests.
The 49% shareholding continuity test applies for loss utilisation; non-resident shareholders must be tracked.
Standard computation; losses cannot be used to offset exempt foreign income.

Apply 28% to taxable income. A non-resident company with no fixed establishment in New Zealand and only New Zealand-source withholding income may have no Box 30 liability if all tax has been satisfied at source.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) paid on dividends, interest, or royalties
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim credits for NRWT withheld at source; attach relevant withholding payment certificates.
Claim RWT credits received on New Zealand-sourced interest or dividends where an NZ bank account is held.
Non-resident companies generally do not operate an ICA unless they elect to be resident and pay imputed dividends to New Zealand resident shareholders.
Disclose any New Zealand government COVID or digital-grant funding, which is taxable where ordinary income principles apply.
Non-resident filers must authorise a tax agent if using third-party filing services; digital signature accepted via myIR.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: NZ$250 immediately for failure to file the IR4, plus NZ$50 per month for each month or part-month thereafter (capped at NZ$500 total late filing penalty per return). Late payment penalties: 1% of unpaid tax on the day after the due date, an additional 4% of unpaid tax two days later, then 1% per month for each month the tax remains unpaid (maximum total late payment penalty 10% of the remaining tax). Use-of-money interest (UOMI) accrues under section 120 of the Tax Administration Act 1994. Shortfall penalties for lack of reasonable care extend up to 20% of the resulting tax shortfall, gross carelessness 40%, and abusive tax position 100%–150%.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: The statutory non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) rate on dividends paid by a New Zealand company to a non-resident shareholder is 15% (Income Tax Act 2007, section 891A). Where a resident company attaches imputation credits, the total tax on a fully imputed dividend is 28%, but the non-resident is still subject to 15% NRWT on the gross dividend; the imputation credits do not reduce the NRWT exposure, but a supplementary dividend regime can fund additional taxation for certain treaty residents. There is no separate dividend distribution tax beyond these rules.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief and reduce the statutory dividend NRWT rate, the non-resident shareholder must: (1) establish eligibility under the specific double tax agreement between New Zealand and the shareholder's country of residence; (2) obtain a Certificate of Residence (CoR) or dedicated tax residence certificate from the home jurisdiction tax authority, covering the dividend payment date and stating beneficial ownership; (3) provide the certificate and a completed IRD Form IR902 to the New Zealand paying company or withholding agent before payment is processed; (4) ensure the shareholder is the beneficial owner of the dividend and satisfies any Limitation on Benefits (LOB) or Principal Purpose Test (PPT) under the relevant DTA and the Multilateral Instrument (MLI); (5) if the reduced treaty rate is not applied at source, the shareholder may apply to Inland Revenue for a refund of excess NRWT within the statutory time bar (four years from the end of the tax year in which the payment is made). Inland Revenue has published operational protocols requiring an approved 'certificate of residence' (Form IR290, IR291, or similar) and may require a specific DwD (double taxation relief) application.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory NRWT for royalties paid by a New Zealand company to a non-resident is 15% (Income Tax Act 2007); statutory NRWT for interest paid to a non-resident is 15%. An Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) of 2% may apply in substitution for NRWT on interest paid to unassociated non-resident lenders under section 86 of the Stamp and Cheque Duties Act 1971, provided the lender is not associated with the borrower. Under New Zealand's double tax agreements, royalty withholding rates vary from 5% to 15%; typical treaty rates are 10% (e.g., NZ–China, NZ–Singapore) and 5% for certain copyright or industrial royalties under some treaties. Interest WHT treaty rates are generally 10% (e.g., NZ–China, NZ–Australia under certain conditions), but may be 0% or 15% depending on treaty identity and whether AIL is used. Relief protocols require a CoR, beneficial ownership confirmation, and relevant treaty article application filed with the withholding agent; where the payer is a non-resident IC, the treaties apply only if the IC is a resident of New Zealand for DTA purposes (i.e., incorporated in NZ and subject to NZ tax, not merely registered).

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand's transfer pricing rules under Subpart GC of the Income Tax Act 2007 incorporate the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines. There is no statutory fixed threshold requiring a formal Local File/Master File. Instead, taxpayers must prepare and retain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation where the aggregate value of cross-border related-party transactions exceeds NZ$1 million for transactions involving goods or services, or NZ$500,000 for financial transactions. Inland Revenue's investigations practice expects a robust TP policy where the volume of related-party dealings is material, and the documentation should include a functional analysis, benchmarking search, and arm's length pricing model. For a low-code SaaS platform generating recurring subscription revenue, transactions with offshore affiliates (e.g., software development, marketing, IP royalty fees) must be benchmarked using accepted methods.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, Profit Split
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not have a separate 'Economic Substance Regulations' statute comparable to UAE/Cayman ESR. However, the general anti-avoidance rule in section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007 and the 'business continuity' and 'source/ordinary income' doctrines require economic substance. For a NZ International Company owned by non-residents, the tax residence test applies the 'centre of management and control' test: if board decisions and day-to-day executive control are exercised in New Zealand, the company is tax-resident and liable at 28% on worldwide income. Thin capitalisation rules under Part FE apply to non-resident-owned companies with New Zealand assets, limiting debt deductions. Inland Revenue can also apply the permanent establishment (PE) concept to attribute New Zealand-sourced business profits, especially where the no-code website builder sells to NZ customers via a local agent or server infrastructure. Substance documentation (physical office, local employees, board meetings) is critical for non-resident ICs to avoid being re-characterised as a NZ-resident company.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately under-reporting web template and SaaS subscription revenue, inflating deductible management fees, or failing to issue tax invoices for no-code website builder services sold to New Zealand customers via Stripe or Paddle payment rails
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under sections 143A and 143B of the Tax Administration Act 1994, tax evasion is a criminal offence: imprisonment for up to five years and a fine of up to NZ$50,000 (first conviction) or NZ$100,000 (subsequent conviction). In addition, shortfall penalties of 20%–150% of the tax shortfall may be imposed (sections 141A–141I TAA). Civil pecuniary penalties of up to NZ$10,000 may also apply.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be prosecuted for aiding and abetting tax evasion. Where the company fails to deduct or remit NRWT or PAYE/income tax, directors can become personally liable under section 31B TAA for unpaid tax and penalties. Courts may impose travel bans, asset restraint orders, and disqualification orders under the Companies Act 1993.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company and Incorrect Tax Residence
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Incorporating a New Zealand IC with no local employees, no physical office, and no substantive decision-making in New Zealand, while the true centre of management and control is exercised in another jurisdiction, in order to claim non-resident status and avoid 28% company tax on global digital revenue
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Inland Revenue may treat the company as a New Zealand-resident company, assess 28% corporate tax on worldwide income, and apply shortfall penalties for lack of reasonable care (up to 40%) or an abusive tax position (up to 150%). The anti-avoidance rule in s BG 1 can void the arrangement. Failure to maintain a local agent or registered office may lead to deregistration under the Companies Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly make false residence declarations or breach the Companies Act face personal liability for unpaid taxes. Directors who fail to exercise proper control can be sued for reckless trading and be personally liable for the company's debts. Travel bans and disqualification orders are available in civil penalty proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Documentation Failure and Profit Shifting
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to prepare contemporaneous TP documentation, setting intercompany royalties at non-arm's length rates, or using the New Zealand entity to bear digital platform development costs while routing all recurring revenue to an offshore affiliate without any functional or risk analysis
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under Subpart GC and OECD TP Guidelines, Inland Revenue may re-assess taxable income at an arm's length profit and apply shortfall penalties of 20%–150% depending on culpability. For failing to keep and maintain sufficient documentation, a specific penalty may be imposed under section 141D TAA (penalty equal to 50% of the resulting tax shortfall if the taxpayer took an unacceptable tax position). Thin capitalisation adjustment causes disallowance of excessive interest deductions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign false TP declarations or fail to ensure the company meets its documentation obligations may be personally liable for shortfall penalties if they are found to have participated in an arrangement with dominant purpose of tax avoidance. Director civil liability applies under company law for insolvent trading.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Non-Resident Withholding Tax Evasion on Profit Repatriation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, royalties, or interest to a non-resident shareholder without deducting NRWT, mischaracterising them as capital account distributions, or channeling payments through a tax-exempt trust or conduit entity to avoid withholding
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The paying company is liable to NRWT at the statutory rate (15% dividends/royalties/interest generally). Late payment penalties (1%+4% initial, plus up to 10% monthly), UOMI, and shortfall penalties apply. Inland Revenue may recover any unreported amount from the directors. Breach of the PAYE/NRWT remittance rules is also a criminal offence under s 144 TAA punishable by imprisonment up to 6 months.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are jointly and severally liable for unremitted NRWT under section 31B TAA when the company has an outstanding deduction obligation and the director fails to take reasonable steps to ensure compliance. Director disqualification and travel bans may be imposed.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Falling within the New Zealand AML/CFT Act 2009 reporting entity category (e.g., providing financial services such as merchant payment facilitation through Stripe or Paddle) and failing to conduct customer due diligence, beneficial ownership verification, and suspicious transaction reporting for high-risk digital payment streams
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, civil penalties for non-compliance range up to NZ$2 million for a body corporate and NZ$200,000 for an individual director/officer. Criminal pecuniary penalties for wilful contravention may reach NZ$5 million for a body corporate and NZ$300,000 for an individual, plus imprisonment up to 2 years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior officers may be personally liable for civil penalties and criminal prosecution if they knowingly allow AML/CFT failures. Personal asset forfeiture or travel bans may be ordered by the High Court. A director can be disqualified under the Companies Act if involved in serious AML/CFT misconduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: False Statutory Filings to Companies Office
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Filing false annual returns or keeping a nominal local agent, failing to disclose significant beneficial ownership changes, or using a nominee director who is unaware of the company's actual business operations, to maintain the appearance of compliance while the company is engaged in undisclosed foreign activity
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Companies Act 1993, knowingly filing false information is an offence punishable by a fine up to NZ$50,000 and imprisonment for up to five years (s 377). Failure to maintain a registered office or agent may cause the Registrar to initiate deregistration, resulting in a dissolved company without the ability to sue or own assets. A false declaration to an AML/CFT regulator also triggers penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign false statutory declarations are personally liable for fines and imprisonment. If the company trades while insolvent and the directors are engaging in fraudulent conduct, personal liability up to the full amount of debts can arise under sections 135, 136 and 588G Companies Act analogues (s 135 reckless trading, s 136 incurring obligations without reasonable belief of solvency).
